The Cape parrot (Poicephalus robustus) is a medium-sized psittacine endemic to the fragmented forests of eastern South Africa, where its life history reflects a relatively slow pace of reproduction compared to other Afrotropical parrots. Females typically produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with clutch sizes most often consisting of three eggs [N_R_i = clutch sizes most often consisting of three eggs], a modest reproductive output that is linked to the extended period of parental care required by the altricial young. The eggs themselves are substantial structures; field measurements have recorded a mean egg length of 3.554 centimeters and a width of 2.866 centimeters, with an estimated fresh egg mass calculated from these dimensions of approximately 7.2 grams. These eggs are incubated for a period of about 31 days [ab = about 31 days] when maintained at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], which aligns with the typical incubation durations reported for other Poicephalus species under controlled captive conditions. The synchrony between the thermal environment of the nest cavity and the physiological requirements of the developing embryo is critical, as deviations from this optimal temperature can significantly impact hatching success.

Upon hatching, the neonates emerge with a wet weight at birth of just 6.5 grams [Wwb = 6.5 grams], a value that represents a tiny fraction of the adult mass and underscores the extreme altriciality characteristic of this genus. The chicks are initially blind, sparsely downed, and entirely dependent on the female for brooding and the male for provisioning. Growth during the early nestling phase is rapid, driven by the high-protein diet of regurgitated seeds and fruits supplied by both parents. The fledging period, marking the time since birth at fledging, occurs at approximately 80 days [tx = approximately 80 days] under the metabolic conditions typical of an active nest environment, which is maintained at a body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C] during brooding. This extended nestling period is one of the longest recorded among parrots of similar body mass, a consequence of the slow maturation of the flight apparatus and the high energetic costs associated with feather synthesis and thermoregulation in the young.

The developmental trajectory following independence continues to be gradual, with the attainment of sexual maturity representing a significant milestone. Puberty, defined as the time since birth at puberty, is reached after approximately 240 days [tp = approximately 240 days] in individuals maintained under conditions that allow for a core body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This relatively late maturation, compared to smaller-bodied parrots, is consistent with the species' life-history strategy of investing heavily in somatic growth before the onset of reproductive function. The ultimate adult wet weight of a fully grown Cape parrot is recorded at 344 grams [Wwi = 344 grams], although considerable variation exists across published records, with field data from the Endangered Wildlife Trust suggesting a range of 260 to 329 grams for free-living individuals. The difference between the captive and wild weight ranges likely reflects the more consistent food availability in aviaries versus the seasonal fluctuations in fruit abundance that wild birds experience in their mistbelt forest habitat.

First successful breeding in the wild is typically deferred until the birds have established a territory and a pair bond, which is energetically demanding. The age at first reproduction, measured as the time since birth at first brood, has been documented at 730 days [tR = 730 days] for captive birds held at a thermoneutral zone of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. In natural populations, this value may be extended further due to the challenges of locating suitable nesting cavities in the large, old yellowwood trees they prefer. The species' maximum recorded longevity in captivity, representing the lifespan, is estimated at approximately 29.7 years [am = approximately 29.7 years] when birds are housed under thermal conditions that permit a stable body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This extended lifespan, far greater than that of comparably sized songbirds, is a classic correlate of a slow life-history pace, featuring high adult survival rates offset by low annual fecundity and extended periods of juvenile dependency.

Assuming a single successful clutch of three eggs per year, the maximum annual reproductive output translates to a value of approximately three offspring per year, with females producing a single clutch per year [F_R_i = a single clutch per year], of three eggs per year [Ri = of three eggs per year] under the stable metabolic conditions afforded by a body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This low intrinsic rate of increase makes the species exceptionally vulnerable to population declines from habitat loss or increased nest predation, as even a small reduction in adult survival can take decades to reverse. The conservation implications of these life-history parameters are profound; the species is currently listed as Endangered, and recovery programs must account for the fact that a pair may require two full years post-fledging to reach their first breeding attempt (730 days since birth) [tR = 730 days since birth] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. Understanding the interplay between these reproductive constraints and the thermal physiology of the species, which operates effectively only within a narrow range around 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], is crucial for modeling population viability under projected climate change scenarios.
